newsitem.title: USA: Exclusive TV footage shows sickly Pol Pot.
newsitem.headline: Exclusive TV footage shows sickly Pol Pot.

text.p: Exclusive U.S. television footage on Monday night of Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot showed a defeated old man in ill health who appeared only mildly interested in a show trial by fellow guerrillas last week.

The television footage, excerpts of which were aired by ABC-TV's "World News Tonight" and "Nightline" programmes, was obtained by Nate Thayer, an American journalist who witnessed the trial in northern Cambodia last Friday.

Pol Pot, dressed in a light green cotton shirt and dark pants, wore a blue and white scarf during the trial and pulled it close around his neck as he was led away after being sentenced to house arrest for the rest of his life.

The dark eyes that flashed in the last television film of Pol Pot made 18 years ago -- just after the Khmer Rouge's "killing fields" rule from 1975-79 -- now appeared dull and tired, his only weapon now a slender wooden cane.
Pol Pot was the architect of that period, when more than a million Cambodians were killed by execution, torture, disease, starvation or hard labour.
ABC's Ted Koppel said Pol Pot suffered from malaria, high blood pressure and heart disease, and did not appear to have long to live.

Thayer, a correspondent with the Far Eastern Economic Review, described the trial as "an extremely surreal historic moment" and said the guerrilla leaders had decided their verdict in advance of the trial after much internal debate.

"In fact, there was a debate within the leadership on whether to ... kill him, cut him off from medical care, or give him the medical care that they could and allow him to live his final days under house arrest," Thayer said.
"They said very clearly that many of the top leadership wanted to execute Pol Pot and the other three under detention," Thayer said.
Three of Pol Pot's generals were also on trial, seated in handcuffs near the former Khmer Rouge leader.

Thayer, the first foreign journalist to see Pol Pot in 18 years, said in a news release on Monday that the trial in front of some 500 Khmer Rouge cadres was clearly stage-managed but he said there was no doubt Pol Pot's downfall was genuine.
Hundreds of young men and women sat crowded in an open-air shed in the jungle, listening intently as a succession of speakers denounced Pol Pot, by far the oldest person there.

"It was... a public humiliation. It was a public denunciation," Thayer told ABC. "It wasn't just a sentencing, it was to denounce and humiliate those that they accused themselves; Pol Pot's top loyalists of unspeakable crimes against his own people."

Khmer Rouge radio first denounced Pol Pot, now almost 70, in mid-June, shortly after a bloody split in the secretive Maoist group's top leadership in which defence chief Son Sen and almost a dozen members of his family were slaughtered.

Pol Pot and three of his commanders were found guilty of murdering Son Sen and his family, of "destroying national reconciliation" and of stealing money from the party, Thayer said. The three commanders were also said to have raped the wives of their comrades, he said.
Koppel said Pol Pot appeared ready to disappear from public view again since he had been condemned to spend the rest of his life under house arrest.
